Senses.PreferredTarget: at the gate of light and shadow
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "at the gate or threshold of light and shadow." The phrase occurs 28 times in 22 allowlisted texts. The corpus supplies its architectural contrast directly: people have not recognized "the coarse, shallow business under the gate of light and shadow" and mistake it for "the matter inside the house" (光影門頭戶底麤淺底事，將作屋裏事). Elsewhere students are said to "recognize only the gate of light and shadow as themselves" (惟認光影門頭當作自己), and an address warns, "do not bury yourself at the gate of light and shadow" (切忌向光影門頭自埋沒). The phrase also enters verse as a place not to stop: "do not halt your steps at the gate of light and shadow" (光影門頭休駐足). Hongzhi supplies a notable counter-deployment: "a person who settles the matter at the gate of light and shadow will do" (光影門頭了事底漢即得), then immediately asks how one proceeds before guest and host divide and before an image is formed. Zen thus bends ordinary light, shadow, and doorway language into a recurring label for the visible or reflected threshold that records contrast with the inside of the house, oneself, and the not-yet-formed image.
Senses.Note: One spatially loaded idiom covers the sampled uses. Warnings, criticisms, and Hongzhi's qualified acceptance are different appraisals of the same light-and-shadow threshold, not different things. The corpus's own gate/inside-house and formed-image/not-yet-formed-image contrasts establish the definition without requiring an added reading.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如今人未認得光影門頭戶底麤淺底事，將作屋裏事又爭得？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage explicitly calls it the coarse, shallow business under the gate of light and shadow and contrasts it with the matter inside the house.

Occurrences.Kwic: 惟認光影門頭當作自己。汾陽禪師亦云：『五位參尋切要知，纖毫纔動即差違。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The criticism says students recognize only the light-and-shadow gate as themselves, then quotes Fenyang on investigating the five positions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 光影門頭休駐足，色聲叢裡好撐睛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says not to halt at the light-and-shadow gate and to open the eyes amid the thicket of forms and sounds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然如是。光影門頭了事底漢即得。祇如賓主未分。影像未具時。如何履踐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi allows a person who settles the matter at the light-and-shadow gate, then asks how one proceeds before guest and host divide and before an image is formed.

Senses.Explanation: Footwear woven from grass or straw. In Chan records the sandals belong especially to going on foot between teachers: “to wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) and “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years” (更買草鞋行脚三十年) make the ordinary shoe part of the institutional life of itinerant inquiry. The object also enters named encounters: Deshan turns his back on the hall, puts on his sandals, and leaves; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head after Nanquan recounts cutting the cat. Huangbo calls “the patriarchs' dark purport” (祖師玄旨) “worn-out straw sandals” (破草鞋) and says bare feet would be better. The corpus records these concrete actions and comparisons without supplying a symbolic gloss for the sandals.
Senses.Note: The exact term occurs 2,237 times in 301 allowlisted texts. High-value shapes are literal footwear, the travel collocations “wear out sandals” and “buy sandals,” the Deshan departure, the Zhaozhou-on-the-head case, and Huangbo's explicit comparison. No independent self-definition was found.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山背却法堂。著草鞋便行
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record's Deshan case: Deshan turns his back on the hall, puts on his straw sandals, and leaves; the head monk later reports the same action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州外歸。泉舉似州。州乃脫履。安頭上而出。泉云。子若在即救得猫兒。無門曰。且道。趙州頂草鞋意作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Gateless Barrier's Nanquan cat case: Zhaozhou removes a sandal, puts it on his head, and exits; Wumen asks about “Zhaozhou carrying the straw sandal on his head.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師玄旨是破草鞋。寧可赤脚不著最好。僧問。如何是佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo's section explicitly compares “the patriarchs' dark purport” to “worn-out straw sandals” and says going barefoot would be best.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師九年面壁。何不慚惶。若恁麼會得。更買草鞋行脚三十年。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A recorded old adept says that if one understands Bodhidharma's nine years facing the wall in that way, one should “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years.”

Senses.Explanation: To slip or misstep (蹉) while passing (過): 'to slip past' or 'to miss it.' The record uses it when someone fails to catch what is directly before him. One recurrent line says, 'by the time you raise an eyebrow, it has already slipped past' (眨上眉毛，早是蹉過). The stock answer 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過) occurs 158 times in 65 texts. Another passage warns not to miss it face-to-face and says that, if one does, one knows only affairs passing before the eyes (切不得當面蹉過；若蹉過，只知事逐眼前過). The near-synonym 'missed it' (錯過) occurs 863 times, including 134 instances of 'missed it face-to-face' (當面錯過). The headword itself occurs 1,340 times in 213 allowlist texts, and the completed form 'let it slip past' (蹉過了) occurs 117 times. In dialogue it can be paired with 'under your heel' (腳跟下), as when a question about why something is under the monk's heel receives the answer 'missed it face-to-face.'
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The dominant collocation is 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過), a recurring answer and verdict; the near-synonym is 'missed it' (錯過).

Occurrences.Kwic: 眨上眉毛，早是蹉過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), entry for Chan Master Tudu Zhice (塗毒智䇿禪師), in a hall address (上堂). The line says that by the time one raises an eyebrow, it has already slipped past (眨上眉毛，早是蹉過).

Occurrences.Kwic: 向上還有事也無？師曰：當面蹉過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Correct Lineage of the Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統), entry for Chan Master Yunbian (雲辯禪師). The stock answer 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過) follows the question whether there is still a further matter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 切不得當面蹉過；若蹉過，只知事逐眼前過
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Monk Tianyin (天隱和尚語錄), recorded sayings at Baoen Chan Cloister (報恩禪院語錄). The warning not to miss it face-to-face (切不得當面蹉過) is paired with affairs passing before the eyes (事逐眼前過).

Occurrences.Kwic: 眨上眉毛蹉過。大似開眼尿床。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Yuanwu Foguo (圓悟佛果禪師語錄), in a hall address (上堂). The stock line says that raising the eyebrow misses it (眨上眉毛蹉過), followed by the comparison to wetting the bed with one's eyes open.

Occurrences.Kwic: 因甚在汝脚跟下？師曰：當面蹉過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), entry for Chan Master Tudu Zhice (塗毒智䇿禪師). In dialogue, 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過) occurs with 'under your heel' (腳跟下).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「蹉過了也。」僧云：「龍蛇易辨，衲子難瞞。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a public exchange, the master gives the completed-form verdict 'you have missed it,' and the monk immediately answers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 日用頭頭休蹉過，急須著眼看如何
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An instruction warns not to miss it in any part of daily activity and immediately tells the addressee to look carefully.

AlternateTargets: a word that turns the case
Senses.Explanation: A turning word (轉語) is a single pivoting response that turns a stuck situation and settles a case. A master demands one — 'lay down a turning word' (下一轉語 / 著一轉語 / 道一轉語) — or supplies one in another's place (代一轉語). The locus classicus is Baizhang's wild fox: an old man, reborn five hundred times as a fox for once telling a student that a person of great conduct 'does not fall into cause-and-effect' (不落因果), begs Baizhang for a turning word said in his place (代一轉語); Baizhang's turning word — 'do not be blind to cause-and-effect' (不昧因果) — frees him. In the case commentaries masters challenge students to produce one: Wumen repeatedly challenges 'if right here you can lay down a turning word...' (若向者裏下得一轉語), and Xuedou invites 'let each Zen guest lay down a turning word' (請禪客各下一轉語). Baling gave his teacher Yunmen three turning words (三轉語) in place of a lineage-heir letter, and Yunmen said that on his memorial day he would simply cite those three and consider the debt repaid. The stakes of the fox case are stated in-corpus: 'answer a turning word wrongly and you fall into a fox's body' (錯答一轉語者，墮野狐身, the Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings 御選語錄, X68n1319); the case's paired answers survive in near parity — 'does not fall into cause-and-effect' (不落因果) 133 allowlist hits, 'not blind to cause-and-effect' (不昧因果) 126. Besides Baling's three, the record names 'Zhaozhou's three turning words shown to the assembly' (趙州示眾三轉語) (Blue Cliff case 96: 'Raised: Zhaozhou showed the assembly three turning words' 舉。趙州示眾三轉語, T48n2003; also X78n1556, J39nB441) — the three lines 'a golden buddha does not get through a furnace, a wooden buddha does not get through fire, a clay buddha does not get through water' (金佛不度爐。木佛不度火。泥佛不度水。) followed by 'the true buddha sits within' (真佛內裏坐) (X80n1565; 金佛不度爐 122 hits in 78 texts).
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide technical sense, shared across houses; no single master owns it. Multi-source across a lamp record (the Wudeng Huiyuan 五燈會元, 'Five Lamps Merged'), a case collection with comments (the Wumenguan 無門關, 'Gateless Checkpoint'), and case commentary (the Blue Cliff Record 碧巖錄), with distinct masters. Zen-allowlist grep counts: 'turning word' (轉語), 1,435 hits in 265 of 462 texts; 'a turning word' (一轉語) 877, 'lay down a turning word' (下一轉語) 185, 'three turning words' (三轉語) 157, 'a turning word in another's place' (代一轉語) 100, 'able to lay down a turning word' (下得一轉語) 88, 'say a turning word' (道一轉語) 16, 'set down a turning word' (著一轉語) 11, 'each lay down a turning word' (各下一轉語) 11, and the compact form 'lay down a turning word' (下轉語), 9.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今請和尚代一轉語。貴脫野狐身。師曰。汝問。老人曰。大修行人還落因果也無。師曰。不昧因果。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Section head names Chan Master Huaihai of Mount Baizhang in Hongzhou (洪州百丈山懷海禪師); the 'master' (師) is Baizhang. The fox-man asks for a turning word said in his place (代一轉語), and Baizhang's turning word is 'do not be blind to cause-and-effect' (不昧因果). The locus classicus of the term. (Wudeng Huiyuan 五燈會元.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 無門曰。且道。趙州頂草鞋意作麼生。若向者裏下得一轉語。便見南泉令不虛行。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 'Wumen says' (無門曰) — Wumen's stock challenge to the reader to produce a turning word, here on the Nanquan-cuts-the-cat / Zhaozhou-puts-sandals-on-his-head case. (Wumenguan, case 14.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 他日老僧忌辰只舉此三轉語。報恩足矣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 'Yunmen says' (雲門云) — Yunmen on the three turning words (三轉語) that his heir Baling Haojian offered him; he vows to cite only these on his memorial day and count the debt of kindness repaid. The three turning words themselves are Baling's. (Blue Cliff Record.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪竇復云。若要清風再復頭角重生。請禪客各下一轉語。問云。扇子既破。還我犀牛兒來。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 'Xuedou again says' (雪竇復云) — Xuedou inviting each Zen guest to lay down a turning word on Yanguan's rhinoceros-fan case: 'the fan is already broken — bring me back the rhinoceros' (扇子既破。還我犀牛兒來). (Blue Cliff Record, case 91.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 今請闍黎別下一轉語。若愜老僧意。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The 'master' (師) is Chan Master Baiyan Mingzhe of Ezhou (鄂州百巖明哲禪師); a live use — he asks a head-monk to lay down another turning word (別下一轉語), promising to share the summer's gruel if it satisfies him. Shows 'lay down a turning word' as an everyday examination move, not only a device of the case collections. (Wudeng Huiyuan 五燈會元.)

Senses.Explanation: Literally “turn” (轉) the “body or self” (身): to turn oneself around, attested 2,135 times in 327 allowlisted texts. The action can be direct bodily narration: Magu turns intending to sit and is struck, while another master turns and immediately walks away. Chan records also build a productive family from the same turning action. Yuanwu defines a “place to turn oneself” by “speak at the place without words; go at the place where going cannot be done” (無言處言得，行不得處行得，謂之轉身處). Hongzhi says one must know a road to turn; another record directly asks what that road is and answers, “you travel in the wild grass; I again enter the deep village” (汝行荒草裏，我又入深村). A monk asks “what is a turning phrase?” (如何是轉身句) and receives a recorded answer. Other addresses say that bright-eyed patch-robed monks have “no road to turn” (轉身無路), or pair turning with shifting step. Literal motion and the road, place, and phrase compounds preserve one turning action; the former targets were paraphrases, not different referents.
Senses.Note: Further collocations include “turn and shift step” (轉身移步), “no road to turn” (轉身無路), and “turn, then…” (轉身便). Later records use “turning phrase” (轉身句) as a label in stylized exchanges, while Zhongfeng criticizes stock phrases called by that name. Compare road to turn (轉身一路), turning phrase (轉身句), place to turn (轉身處), and shifting step (移步).

Occurrences.Kwic: 若向無言處言得。行不得處行得。謂之轉身處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's Blue Cliff prose: "speak at the place without words; go at the place where going cannot be done—this is called a place to turn oneself."

Occurrences.Kwic: 更須知有轉身一路始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi says: "one must further know that there is a road to turn oneself."

Occurrences.Kwic: 轉身移步若能行，荊棘林中活卓卓。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Feiyin's verse: "if one can turn oneself and shift step, [one is] vividly alive in the thorn forest." No validated roster link is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 谷轉身擬坐，師便打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Raised Linji–Magu exchange: “Magu turned, intending to sit; the master immediately struck him.” Two actors, so unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是轉身句？」師云：「六月炎天冰似火。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks “what is a turning phrase?” and the master answers, “in the sixth-month blazing sky, ice is like fire.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 明眼衲僧轉身無路，現前大眾便合休機
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address says that bright-eyed patch-robed monks have “no road to turn,” followed by an address to the present assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師轉身便行。上堂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After an interlocutor presses for another statement, the master turns and immediately walks away; the record then opens a new hall address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 更須知有轉身一路始得。如何是轉身一路？汝行荒草裏，我又入深村。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record says one must know a road to turn, asks what it is, and supplies the answer, “you travel in the wild grass; I again enter the deep village.”
